n: A rebellion forms. Korah is a Levite, a cousin of Moses and Aaron through Kohath; Dathan, Abiram, and On come from Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn. Both groups may have felt passed over for leadership.

f.g: The Levite clan that carried the holiest furnishings of the tabernacle (Numbers 4:4-15).

n: They are joined by 250 well-known community leaders. This was not a fringe protest but a serious challenge from respected men.

f.g: Chiefs or leaders chosen from the congregation.
Famous, well-regarded men.

n: Their argument sounds spiritual: everyone is holy, so why should Moses and Aaron be above anyone else? But they twist a true idea (Israel is a holy people) into a denial that God calls specific leaders.

f.w: Ye take too much upon you
f.g: “You have gone too far” — you claim more authority than you should.

n: Moses’ first response is not anger but humility: he falls on his face before God.
Moses refuses to settle the matter himself. Tomorrow the Lord will show whom He has chosen. Priesthood authority comes from God’s call, not human campaign.

f.g: shew = show

n: Moses proposes a test: Korah’s group should bring censers, the pans used to burn incense in priestly worship.

f.g: Metal fire-pans for carrying hot coals and burning incense — a duty reserved for priests.

n: Offering incense was the work of priests. Whoever the Lord accepts will be shown to be holy. Moses turns their own words back on them: “Ye take too much upon you.”
Moses now speaks directly to Korah and his fellow Levites.

f.g: A polite “please.”

n: Is it not enough, Moses asks, that God already set the Levites apart to serve at His tabernacle? They had a sacred calling but were not content with it.

f.w: Seemeth it but a small thing unto you
f.g: “Does it seem a small thing to you?”

n: Here is the real issue: Korah wants the priesthood office given to Aaron’s family. Latter-day Saints may recognize the difference between callings and offices — each has its place.
Rebelling against God’s chosen servants is really rebelling against God. Aaron is only a servant; their complaint is against the One who called him.

f.g: Grumble or complain, especially in rebellion.

n: Moses summons Dathan and Abiram, but they flatly refuse to come.

f.g: Likely to come before Moses at the tabernacle; the refusal itself is defiance.

n: Their complaint stuns: they call Egypt — the land of slavery — a land of milk and honey! They accuse Moses of dragging them out to die so he can rule them.

f.g: A phrase God used for Canaan; they reapply it to Egypt, turning God’s promise upside down.

n: They mock Moses for failing to deliver the promised land — forgetting it was their own unbelief that delayed it. “Put out the eyes” likely means “Do you think you can blind these men to the truth?”

f.w: wilt thou put out the eyes of these men?
f.g: An idiom: “Will you fool these men?” or “Will you treat us as blind?”

n: Moses is deeply angry and asks God not to accept their offering. He defends his honesty: he never took so much as a donkey from them.

f.g: wroth = angry

f.w: I have not taken one ass from them

n: Moses repeats the challenge: Korah, his followers, and Aaron must all appear before the Lord tomorrow.
Each of the 250 men, Korah, and Aaron is to bring a censer with incense. Side by side, God will make His choice plain.
The challengers came, censers lit, and stood at the tabernacle entrance alongside Moses and Aaron.

f.g: The tent of meeting, where God met with His people.

n: Korah rallies the whole congregation to his side. At that moment the glory of the Lord appears to everyone — God Himself is about to answer.
The Lord speaks to Moses and Aaron.
God warns Moses and Aaron to step away, for He is about to destroy the whole assembly that sided with Korah.

f.g: Destroy completely, as fire consumes.

n: Moses and Aaron plead for the people. They call God “the God of the spirits of all flesh” — the Father of every spirit — and ask Him not to punish everyone for one man’s sin.

f.w: God of the spirits of all flesh
shall one man sin, and wilt thou be wroth with all the congregation?

n: The Lord answers their intercession. Their plea for mercy changes what happens next — prayer matters.
Rather than destroying everyone, God tells the people to move away from the tents of the three ringleaders. Mercy makes room for separation.

f.g: Here “tabernacle” means the dwelling tents of these men, not the Lord’s tabernacle.

n: Moses goes personally to the tents of Dathan and Abiram — the men who refused to come to him — followed by the elders.
Moses urges everyone to separate from the rebels and touch nothing of theirs. Sin can draw in those who linger near it.
The people pull back on every side. Dathan and Abiram stand defiantly at their tent doors with their families.

f.g: gat = got (moved, went)

n: Moses states the test plainly: what is about to happen will prove that he did not invent his calling. God sent him.
If these men die a normal death, then Moses is not God’s messenger.

f.w: visited after the visitation of all men
f.g: If they meet the ordinary fate everyone meets.

n: But if God does something unheard of — the earth opening to swallow them alive — everyone will know these men have provoked the Lord.

f.g: quick = alive
Hebrew Sheol — the place of the dead, pictured as deep in the earth.
appertain = belong

n: As soon as Moses finished speaking, the ground split open beneath them.

f.g: clave asunder = split apart

n: The earth swallowed the rebels, their households, Korah’s men, and their goods. Numbers 26:11 notes that Korah’s own sons did not die — later their descendants wrote several Psalms.
They went down alive into the pit, and the ground closed over them. Their rebellion ended in being removed from the congregation they had tried to lead.
Terrified by the screams, the people ran, afraid the earth would swallow them too.
Then fire came from the Lord and consumed the 250 men offering incense — the very act by which they had claimed the priesthood.

f.w: there came out a fire from the LORD

n: The Lord gives instructions about what remains.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son and a priest, is to gather the censers from the ashes and scatter the coals. The censers had been offered before the Lord, so they had become holy objects.

f.g: hallowed = made holy, set apart for God
yonder = over there, at a distance

n: The bronze censers are to be hammered into a covering for the altar — a permanent reminder. The men had sinned “against their own souls”: rebellion ultimately harms the rebel most.

f.g: They forfeited their own lives through their sin.

n: Eleazar does as commanded, turning the censers into plates for the altar.

f.g: brasen = made of bronze (brass)

n: Every time Israel saw the altar, they would remember: only those called through Aaron’s line could offer incense. Authority must be given by God.

f.g: Here, anyone outside Aaron’s priestly family, even an Israelite.

f.w: that no stranger, which is not of the seed of Aaron, come near to offer incense

n: Astonishingly, the very next day the whole community blames Moses and Aaron for the deaths. Hearts hardened by murmuring rarely learn quickly.

f.g: on the morrow = the next day

n: As the crowd gathers against them, the cloud covers the tabernacle and God’s glory appears again.
Moses and Aaron go to the front of the tabernacle.
Once more the Lord speaks to Moses, this time about the crowd that has turned against him.
Again God warns that He will destroy the people, and again Moses and Aaron fall to the ground — interceding rather than fleeing.
Moses acts quickly: Aaron must take fire from the altar, add incense, and rush into the crowd to make atonement, because a plague has started.

f.g: Here the incense represents prayer and intercession that turns away judgment.

n: Aaron runs into the midst of the dying people — the same people who had just accused him — offering incense on their behalf.
Aaron stands between the dead and the living, and the plague stops. It is a powerful picture of Jesus Christ, the great High Priest, who stands between us and death.

f.w: he stood between the dead and the living

f.g: stayed = stopped, held back

n: Some 14,700 died in the plague, in addition to those who died with Korah. The numbers underline the cost of spreading rebellion.
Aaron returns to Moses at the tabernacle, and the plague has ended. His humble intercession — not Korah’s ambition — showed who truly held the priesthood.
